response.answer: Lightweight variants have fewer parameters, lower FLOPs, less peak memory, and higher inference latency; mid-range have more; full-scale have the most resources and lowest latency.

results.title: EdgeProfiler: A Fast Profiling Framework for Lightweight LLMs on Edge Using Analytical Model
results.content: Large Language Models, LLM, TinyML, Edge Computing, Quantization, Low-Power Devices, Microcontrollers. However, these models typically require substantial computational resources, memory, and power, which confine their deployment to cloud environments equipped with high-performance servers and GPUs. Despite these challenges, there is growing interest in implementing LLMs on edge devices, including microcontrollers and low-power platforms. This has led to an active area of research focused on quantization techniques, model pruning, and efficient inference strategies that adapt LLMs to the limitations of edge hardware [5]. It shows that aggressive quantization makes lightweight LLMs practical for edge deployment by reducing memory, computation, and energy costs with only minor accuracy trade-offs. Post-training quantization techniques, such as GPTQ  [12], compress model weights to as low as 2–4 bits, balancing memory efficiency and accuracy. The analysis covers multiple numeric precisions (FP32, FP16, INT8) and representative 1–1.5B parameter LLMs. For each configuration, the profiler outputs key metrics, including parameter count, FLOPs per token, peak memory footprint, stage-wise latency (compute, memory, I/O, H2D, network), end-to-end latency, arithmetic intensity, and energy per token.

results.title: LLM Compute, Performance, Cost and Power analysis in a spreadsheet
results.content: # LLM Compute, Performance, Cost and Power analysis in a spreadsheet. The power of Large Language Models is undeniable, but so is their computational complexity and inference cost is increasing due to greater output tokens with greater use of reasoning models. Agentic AI promises to increase the demand for inference compute dramatically. To cut through the opacity, I've developed a detailed spreadsheet-based LLM compute tool, available to anyone for free, see below. Its goal: to sharpen understanding of LLM architectures, meticulously quantify their compute (FLOPs) and memory demands, and empower clear comparisons of performance (tokens/s, latency, power) and economics ($/token) across diverse LLMs and GPUs. This is a preview of an example set of inputs (in green) and core outputs (in pink) of the tool. * AI Leaders & Strategists: Understand how LLM cost of inference changes with workload, how to convert your GPU $/hr costs into token/s depending on the model, thereby knowing how much aggregate load you can serve. * LLM Learners & AI/ML Engineers:  Know every matmul in an LLM, compare the different open model architectures, quantify the impact of optimizations like KV Cache, MoE, 16bit vs 8bit models, know the memory and FLOP needs of any open source model. * GPU Vendors and Architects: Use the detailed matrix multiplication sequences and memory bandwidth needs to inform next-generation microarchitecture of GPUs, find the right balance of FLOPs to memory bandwidth for target models, benchmark your GPU vs others. * Architectural choices are paramount: The Llama 4 Maverick 400B model, for instance, shows significantly higher aggregate throughput – approximately 8x that of Deepseek v3 670B (on Ascend/H200/B200) and about 2x Qwen3 235B (across various GPUs). Memory movement is the key to model inference cost. The tool data shows that LLM inference is memory bound for the above models. This detailed, first-principles modeling is what enables precise performance predictions, architectural comparisons, and cost analyses critical for anyone deploying or developing LLMs. Future work includes modeling of inter-GPU communication and synchronization overheads. #LLM #AI #GenAI #MachineLearning #DeepLearning #GPU #Nvidia #PerformanceModeling #Llama #Deepseek #Qwen #FoundationModels. * ### GPU vs TPU: ARCHITECTURE, PERFORMANCE, COST, ECOSYSTEM & IMPLICATIONS FOR SOVEREIGN AI.

results.title: Understanding Evaluation parameters for Object Detection Models — Flops, FPS, Latency, Params, Size, Memory, Storage, mAP, AP | by Nikita Malviya | Medium
results.content: # Understanding Evaluation parameters for Object Detection Models — Flops, FPS, Latency, Params, Size, Memory, Storage, mAP, AP. In this blog, we will be discussing **the parameters that are used to evaluate the performance of different models**, commonly object detection models. FPS represents **the number of frames an object detection model can process per second**. Average Precision is a widely used **metric** **for** **evaluating the accuracy** of object detection models. A crucial metric for **measuring the accuracy** of object detection models. * **Higher** **mAP**: Indicates **better overall accuracy** in detecting and positioning objects. * **mAP-50:** Focuses on how well the model detects objects with **moderate overlap**. * **mAP-75:** Emphasizes the model’s ability to detect objects with **high overlap**, typically representing **tightly packed or closely positioned objects**. * **Higher** **mAP-R:** indicates **better** **performance** in **detecting objects across a range of aspect ratios.**. Memory:** More complex models with higher accuracy require more memory storage. These parameters provide valuable insights into the performance and limitations of object detection models.

results.title: Planetary-Scale Inference: Previewing our Peer-To-Peer Decentralized Inference Stack
results.content: * Surprisingly, asynchronous micro-batch pipeline schedules (like ZeroBubble) are effective for compute-bound workloads like training but not for inference workloads, which are typically bounded by memory bandwidth and total memory. + The KV cache's high memory demands grow with parallel sequence decoding, preventing compute-bound operation (which would occur at $B\_{crit}$). + Consider $N$ devices running either a synchronous schedule with $B\_{max}$ or an asynchronous schedule with $N$ micro-batches of size $B\_{max}/N$: Due to linear throughput scaling, processing either the full batch or a micro-batch takes time $T$. When running operations on accelerators, three factors determine the total latency: computation time for processing FLOPs, memory communication time for moving data between memory and compute cores, and network communication time between hosts. * **Memory Bandwidth-Bound** ($T\_{\text{mem}}>T\_{\text{comp}}, T\_{\text{net}}$): Most time is spent moving data to and from memory - compute and network sit idle. For operations running on a single accelerator (no network communication), a good way to tell if an operation is likely compute or memory-bandwidth bound is to look at its FLOPS per byte, sometimes called the *operation intensity*, defined as. $$\text{Intensity}(\textsf{Accelerator})=\frac{\text{Compute Speed [FLOPs/s]}}{\text{Memory Bandwidth [Bytes/s]}}$$. Getting an idea of whether we are compute or memory bandwidth-bound in these two operations will allow us to lower bound the time it takes for one prefill and decode step. $$B\_{max}:=\left\lfloor\frac{\text{Accelerator Memory}-\text{Model Size}-C}{T\cdot \text{KV Cache Size}}\right\rfloor$$. As we have seen, $T(\textsf{Linear})$ may be compute-bound or memory-bandwidth bound during decode, depending on the batch size $B$ used. $$T\_{\text{mem}}(\textsf{Attention})=\frac{B\cdot T\cdot \text{KV Cache Size}}{2 \cdot \text{Memory Bandwidth [Bytes/s]}}$$. $$\text{Throughput/PP} = \frac{B}{\text{Step Time/PP}} \leq \frac{B}{N \cdot \text{Network Latency}}$$. Unfortunately, for as long as we are memory bandwidth-bound, instead of compute-bound (which we are during decoding), we have that the time to process a micro-batch is roughly the same as the time to process a full batch, let's denote this as time $T$. This is because we are memory-bandwidth bound, so increasing the batch size yields "free" throughput gains because the operation time is dominated by moving parameters, not the actual computation. Asynchronous micro-batched pipeline schedules cannot increase throughput for memory bandwidth-bound workloads, like decoding during inference.

results.title: Model GPU memory requirements
results.content: `KV cache memory (bytes) ~= B * (2 * n_layers * n_heads * d_head * t_seq_len * p_a)`. `Activation memory (bytes) ~= B * t_seq_len * E * C`. `Total Memory (bytes) = Model weights + KV cache + Activation + Overhead`. Model weights and kv cache account for ~90% of total GPU memory requirements during inference. `Total Memory (bytes) ~= Model weights + (No of Tokens * Memory per Token)`. * higher throughput means maximizing memory bandwidth utilization & MFU (model FLOPS utilization). * Total model memory ~= model weights + kv cache size. # A10 - Llama 7B Total FLOPs & Inference time. Total model memory ≈ model weights + kv cache size. ### Insights from Model Latency & Understanding Hardware Utilization on Modern GPUs. Since decode phase dominates FLOPS & HBM bandwidth, transformer inference is almost always bandwidth limited (memory bound). Improvements in model algorithms like Flash Attention result in efficient memory bandwidth utilization and also FLOPS utilization.
